intro: Linking words join ideas and turn a list of short sentences into real speech. “And” adds, “but” shows a contrast, “because” gives a reason, and “or” gives a choice. Using them well makes your English smoother and more natural.
objectifs: Join two ideas with and (adding), but (contrast) and because (reason).
Use or for a choice and in negative sentences.
Write a correct list (A, B and C) with commas.
Know the difference between because (+ subject + verb) and because of (+ noun).

texte: “And” adds information. It joins two words, two groups or two sentences: “bread and butter”, “I get up and I have a shower”.
When the subject is the same, you don't need to repeat it: “I get up and have a shower.”

In a list, separate the items with commas and put “and” before the last one: “I speak French, English and Ewondo.” In American English, people often put a comma before “and” too (“French, English, and Ewondo”): this is the “Oxford comma”.
exemples: My sister is a nurse and my brother is a teacher.
I buy tomatoes, onions and rice.
She finishes work and goes to the gym.

texte: “But” shows a contrast or a surprise. We often put a comma before “but” when it joins two full sentences: “The hotel is small, but it's very nice.”
Don't use “but” when there is no contrast: “I like cats and I like dogs too.” (not “but”).
In more formal English, you will later use “however” and “although” (lesson 118).
exemples: I like my job, but it's very tiring.
The flat is small but bright.
He can speak English, but he can't write it.

texte: “Because” gives a reason. It is followed by a subject and a verb: “I'm tired because I work at night.” It is the natural answer to “Why?”.
“Because of” is followed by a noun: “The train is late because of the snow.” Compare: “because it's snowing” / “because of the snow”.

In speech, you can answer “Because I'm tired.” alone. In writing, don't write a sentence that starts with “Because” and has no main part; write “I'm staying at home because I'm tired.” or “Because I'm tired, I'm staying at home.”

lignes: Why are you late? — Because the bus is late.

exemples: I'm learning English because I want to work in Canada.
We're staying at home because of the storm.
sections.note: In informal speech, “because” often becomes “'cause” or “cos” /kəz/. Don't write it in a formal text.

texte: “Or” gives a choice: “Tea or coffee?”, “We can walk or take a taxi.”
In a negative sentence, English uses “or”, not “and”: “I don't like tea or coffee.” (I don't like either of them.) “I don't like tea and coffee” sounds wrong or changes the meaning.
For the opposite of “because” (the result), use “so”: “It's raining, so I'm taking an umbrella.” Lesson 75 looks at so, then, after that.
exemples: Do you want to stay here or go out?
She doesn't eat meat or fish.

texte: With these words you go from very short sentences (“I live in Liège. I like it. It's rainy.”) to more natural speech: “I live in Liège and I like it, but it's often rainy.”
But don't make very long sentences with five “and”s: in writing, two clear sentences are better.
exemples: I love Brussels because it's international, but the weather isn't great.
We can go to the beach or visit the museum, and then have dinner.

formule: A and B (adding) · A, but B (contrast) · A because B (reason) · A or B (choice; negatives)
prononciation: “and” is almost always weak: /ən/ or even /n/. “fish and chips” = /ˌfɪʃ n ˈtʃɪps/, “rock and roll” = “rock'n'roll”.
“but” is weak in the middle of a sentence: /bət/. It is strong /bʌt/ when you want to stress it.
“because” is /bɪˈkɒz/ (UK) or /bɪˈkʌz/ (US), with the stress on the second syllable. In fast speech: /kəz/.
In a list, the voice goes up on each item and down on the last: “tomatoes ↗, onions ↗ and rice ↘”.
In a choice question, the voice goes up on the first choice and down on the second: “Tea ↗ or coffee ↘?”.
erreurs: I don't like tea and coffee.
I don't like tea or coffee.
In a negative sentence: “or”.
I'm late because the traffic.
I'm late because of the traffic.
Before a noun: “because of”.
I'm tired because of I work a lot.
I'm tired because I work a lot.
Before subject + verb: “because”.
I like cats but I like dogs too.
I like cats and I like dogs too.
No contrast: “and”.
Do you want tea and coffee? (a choice)
Do you want tea or coffee?
For a choice: “or”.
She speaks English, French, Spanish.
She speaks English, French and Spanish.
“and” before the last item in a list.
Because I'm ill. (alone, in an email)
I can't come to work today because I'm ill.
In writing, “because” needs a main part.

dialogue.contexte: In Abidjan, Koffi phones his friend Mariam to plan the weekend.
lignes: Hi Mariam! Are you free on Saturday?
In the morning, no, because I work. But I'm free in the afternoon.
Great! We can go to the beach or watch a film.
The beach! I love the sea and it's very hot this week.
OK. Let's take the bus, because my car is at the garage.
No problem. Can I bring my sister? She's on holiday and she's bored.
Of course! But she doesn't swim, right?
No, she can't swim, but she loves sitting in the sun and reading.

mots: used to join words or ideas
It's late, so I'm going home.
as well (at the end of a sentence)

exercices.consigne: Make one sentence with and, but or because.
items: I'm hungry. I want a sandwich.
I'm hungry and I want a sandwich.
I like Lyon. It's expensive.
I like Lyon, but it's expensive.
She's tired. She works at night.
She's tired because she works at night.
He speaks French. He speaks English.
He speaks French and English.
The shop is closed. It's Sunday.
The shop is closed because it's Sunday.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: I don't like tea and coffee.
I don't like tea or coffee.
The train is late because the snow.
The train is late because of the snow.
I'm learning English because of I want to travel.
I'm learning English because I want to travel.
The hotel is small and comfortable but cheap and nice.
The hotel is small but comfortable. (or: The hotel is small, cheap and comfortable.)
Do you want juice and water? (a choice)
Do you want juice or water? / Would you like juice or water?

exercices.consigne: Write four or five sentences about your town or your job. Use and, but, because and or at least once.
items: Model answer

I live in Douala and I work in a bank. I like my job because my colleagues are friendly, but the days are long. After work I go to the gym or I visit my parents. I'm learning English because I want a job in Canada.

a_retenir: and = adding; in a list: A, B and C.
but = contrast (often with a comma before it); no “but” without a contrast.
because + subject + verb (because it's raining); because of + noun (because of the rain).
or = choice; in a negative sentence: I don't like tea or coffee.
so = result (It's late, so I'm going home).
